LightGCN: Implementation, Evaluation, Layer Adaptation & Contrastive Learning

A Scientific Investigation into Graph Convolutional Collaborative Filtering, Adaptive Layer Aggregation, and Gradient Dynamics in Contrastive Objectives
PyTorch 2.0+ 33 Unit Tests Passed MovieLens-100K Benchmark 5 Model Variants & Multi-Seed Protocol
Executive Summary

This technical report documents the complete mathematical formulation, modular software engineering, empirical verification, and architectural extensions of LightGCN (He et al., SIGIR 2020) and its contrastive learning adaptations inspired by SimpleX (Mao et al., CIKM 2021). Through systematic multi-seed controlled experimentation on MovieLens-100K, we demonstrate that collaborative filtering performance is fundamentally bottlenecked by the choice of loss objective and negative sampling ratio rather than graph encoder complexity:

  • Baseline LightGCN (BPR, 1 negative): Achieves 0.2693 Recall@20 and 0.1849 NDCG@20.
  • AdaptiveLightGCN (Trainable Softmax Aggregation): Learns non-uniform propagation weights favoring intermediate layers (k=1, 2), improving Recall@20 to 0.2851 (+5.9% relative gain).
  • LightGCN-CCL (Hinge Cosine Contrastive Loss, 50 negatives): Scales negative sampling with directional cosine scoring, boosting Recall@20 to 0.3464 (+28.6% relative gain over baseline).
  • LightGCN-Softmax (Sampled InfoNCE Contrastive Loss, τ=0.15): Eliminates the 81.5% zero-gradient dead zone of hinge loss via continuous, smooth competitive repulsion, achieving 0.3693 Recall@20 and 0.2658 NDCG@20 (+37.1% and +43.8% relative gains over baseline LightGCN).

1 Theoretical Foundations: Recommender Systems on Graphs

Collaborative filtering platforms record binary user-item interactions (clicks, purchases, ratings ≥ 3), representing observed positive feedback. Unobserved entries do not imply negative preferences; they primarily represent unexposed candidates.

1.1 User-Item Bipartite Graph & Degree Normalization

Let M denote the number of users and N the number of items. The interaction topology forms an undirected bipartite graph G = (V, E) with total vertices |V| = M + N. The bipartite adjacency matrix A is defined as:

A = [ 0 R RT 0 ] ∈ ℝ(M+N) × (M+N)
(Eq. 1)

Standard Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) suffer from node-degree scale divergence. LightGCN applies symmetric degree-based normalization:

Ã = D-1/2 A D-1/2,   Ãu, M+i = 1 / (√|Nu| √|Ni|)
(Eq. 2)

1.2 Light Graph Convolution (LGC) & Mitigation of Oversmoothing

Conventional GCNs (e.g., NGCF) employ heavy weight transformation matrices W and non-linear activations σ(x). The seminal insight of LightGCN is that node features in collaborative filtering are simply categorical IDs with no inherent semantic features. Feature transformation and non-linearities degrade recommendation performance and make training unstable. LightGCN strips away all non-linearities and parameter matrices, distilling graph convolution down to pure linear neighborhood smoothing:

E(0) = [P; Q] ∈ ℝ(M+N) × d,   E(k+1) = Ã E(k)
(Eq. 3)

To alleviate oversmoothing (the tendency of node embeddings to collapse into identical averages across deeper layers), multi-layer representations are combined into a final representation:

E* = ∑k=0K αk E(k),   eu* = ∑k=0K αk eu(k),   ei* = ∑k=0K αk ei(k)
(Eq. 4)

2 End-to-End System Architecture

The modular framework maps directly from raw implicit interactions to graph construction, multi-layer propagation, scoring heads, and loss optimization:

Figure 1: End-to-end architectural system diagram. (1) Raw interaction tuples are preprocessed with leak-free stratified splitting. (2) Sparse bipartite adjacency matrix is normalized symmetrically. (3) Light Graph Convolution performs linear smoothing over K=3 propagation layers. (4) Layer combination aggregates representations using uniform weights (Baseline/CCL) or trainable softmax logits (Adaptive). (5) Scoring heads evaluate dot-product or cosine similarity against full item candidate pools with training item masking. (6) Objectives optimize mini-batches using BPR, Hinge CCL, or Cosine Softmax Contrastive Loss.

3 Loss Function Mechanics & The Hinge Dead Zone

The project evaluates three fundamentally distinct loss mechanisms to train the LightGCN encoder:

3.1 Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR) Loss

Standard LightGCN relies on BPR pairwise loss with inner-product scoring ŷui = (eu*)T ei*. Only a single negative item j is sampled per positive item i:

LBPR = - (1/|B|) ∑(u,i,j) ln σ(ŷui - ŷuj) + (λ/2|B|) ∑ (||eu(0)||2 + ||ei(0)||2 + ||ej(0)||2)
(Eq. 5)

3.2 SimpleX Cosine Contrastive Loss (CCL)

Mao et al. (CIKM 2021) identified two critical flaws in BPR: dot products suffer from severe node popularity bias (unbounded embedding magnitudes), and 1 negative sample per positive provides insufficient coverage of the unobserved space. CCL enforces directional alignment on the unit hypersphere and scales negative sampling (|N| ≥ 50):

LCCL(u, i) = (1 - yui) + (w / |N|) ∑j ∈ N max(0, yuj - m)
(Eq. 6)

3.3 The Hinge Dead Zone & Continuous Softmax Contrastive Loss

While Hinge CCL dramatically outperforms BPR, representation diagnostics revealed a severe limitation: 81.5% of sampled negatives have similarity below the margin threshold (yuj < 0.8), yielding an exact zero gradient: ∂LCCL / ∂yuj = 0. Over four-fifths of the sampled negative items provide zero learning signal!

Figure 2: Theoretical gradient repulsion mechanisms & empirical dead zone distribution. Left: Repulsive gradient magnitude |∂L/∂yuj| plotted against negative sample cosine similarity. Hinge CCL exhibits a hard cutoff at margin m (zero gradient for all easy negatives). In contrast, Cosine Softmax provides smooth, continuous repulsive gradients across the entire similarity spectrum. Right: Empirical histogram of negative sample cosine similarities under trained LightGCN-CCL (m=0.8), proving that 81.5% of negatives reside in the inactive dead zone.

To resolve the dead zone, we formulated Cosine Softmax Contrastive Loss (sampled InfoNCE):

Lsoftmax = - (1/|B|) ∑(u,i) ∈ B ln [ exp(cos(eu*, ei*) / τ) / (exp(cos(eu*, ei*) / τ) + ∑j ∈ Nu exp(cos(eu*, ej*) / τ)) ]
(Eq. 7)

Under Cosine Softmax, the negative repulsive gradient is -puj / τ. Because the softmax probability puj > 0 everywhere, every single unobserved negative sample exerts continuous repulsive pressure, dynamically scaling with its hardness.

4 Controlled Multi-Seed Empirical Results (MovieLens-100K)

All five model variants were trained under identical conditions (15 epochs, batch size 1024, embedding dimension 64, 3 GCN propagation layers, Adam optimizer with lr=0.001) across multiple random seeds (42 and 123) on the official MovieLens-100K stratified split. Evaluation ranks all unobserved candidates across the entire item catalog with observed training items masked to -∞.

5.1 Angular Separation on the Unit Hypersphere

We extracted user and item representations from the trained checkpoints on the test set and computed Kernel Density Estimations (KDE) of positive user-item similarity vs unobserved negative similarity:

Figure 7: Empirical cosine similarity KDE distributions on the unit hypersphere. Baseline & Adaptive: Suffer from representation overlap and weak directional discrimination. LightGCN-CCL (m=0.8): Forces unobserved negatives to pile up immediately below the margin boundary at mean similarity +0.76 (separation margin Δ = 0.047). LightGCN-Softmax (τ=0.15): Drives unobserved negatives into a wide, uniform distribution with mean -0.07 while maintaining positive alignment at +0.22, establishing a massive angular separation margin of Δ = 0.290.

6.2 Comprehensive Verification Suite (33 Unit Tests)

The codebase is protected by a complete suite of 33 unit tests executing in under 5 seconds:

  • tests/test_graph.py (3 tests): Bipartite adjacency structure, symmetry, and degree normalization D-1/2 A D-1/2.
  • tests/test_model.py (2 tests): Exact linear graph convolution propagation mathematics and recommendation scoring.
  • tests/test_adaptive_model.py (3 tests): Softmax parameter initialization (θ=0), baseline equivalence, and gradient flow.
  • tests/test_loss.py (2 tests): Pairwise BPR margin ordering and layer-0 L2 regularization scaling.
  • tests/test_ccl_loss.py (8 tests): Hand-calculated numerical examples, zero-penalty below margin, linear penalty above margin, |N| normalization, numerical stability, and cosine softmax contrastive loss.
  • tests/test_sampler.py (6 tests): Negative sampling validity, strict train positive exclusion, dense-user edge cases.
  • tests/test_metrics.py (2 tests): Full-candidate ranking, candidate masking (-∞), hand-verified Recall@K and NDCG@K.
  • tests/test_dataset.py (3 tests): ID remapping, deduplication, and leak-free stratified splitting.
  • tests/test_lightgcn_ccl.py (3 tests): End-to-end toy forward pass, optimizer step, and finite evaluation metrics.
  • tests/test_reproducibility.py (1 test): Multi-seed determinism and exact reproducibility.

To generate personalized Top-5 recommendations for any user using the trained checkpoint: 

import torch
from src.dataset import InteractionData
from src.graph import build_torch_normalized_adjacency
from src.models.lightgcn_ccl import LightGCNCCL
from scripts.train_baseline import load_dataset

# 1. Load dataset and construct normalized adjacency
data = load_dataset("data/ml-100k")
norm_adj = build_torch_normalized_adjacency(data.num_users, data.num_items, data.train_pairs)

# 2. Instantiate model and load trained best checkpoint
model = LightGCNCCL(num_users=data.num_users, num_items=data.num_items, embedding_dim=64, num_layers=3, score_type="cosine")
ckpt = torch.load("experiments/comparison/lightgcn_softmax_tau015_seed_42/best_model.pt", map_location="cpu")
model.load_state_dict(ckpt["model_state_dict"])
model.eval()

# 3. Predict all candidate scores and mask seen training items
with torch.no_grad():
    scores = model.predict_all_for_users(torch.tensor([0]), norm_adj)[0]
seen = data.train_user_positives.get(0, set())
if seen: scores[list(seen)] = -float("inf")

# 4. Retrieve Top-5 recommendation rankings
top_scores, top_items = torch.topk(scores, 5)
for rank, (item_idx, score) in enumerate(zip(top_items.tolist(), top_scores.tolist()), 1):
    print(f"Rank {rank}: Item Index {item_idx:4d} | Cosine Score: {score:.4f}")
